title: the Rudram
hook: the Rudram looks up at the sun crossing the sky, copper and red, and says the cowherds have seen him

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rudram opened with a bow to anger and asked Rudra to unstring the bow.

Early morning in a village. A boy drives cattle out to graze. A woman walks back from the well with a water pot on her hip. Neither is a priest, and neither is chanting anything. The sun comes up over the fields, copper, then red, then a warm brown glow. Still in its opening section, the Rudram points at that sun. That one, it says. The cowherds have seen him. The women carrying water have seen him.
screen: `A BOY WITH CATTLE.` → `A WOMAN WITH A WATER POT.` → `THE SUN COMING UP.`

segments.voice: The verses describe a figure in the sky: copper-colored, and red, and brown, and wholly auspicious. Around him, the hymn says, are more Rudras on every side, and it asks that their anger be turned aside. Then it describes him moving across the sky, the one with the blue throat, glowing red. And then the surprising line. The cowherds have seen him. The water-carrying women have seen him. All beings have seen him. May he, seen, be kind to us. Some readers, following the old commentary, take this figure as the sun crossing the sky. On that reading, Rudra isn't hidden in a cave or locked in a temple. He's in plain view, every morning. And the people named as having seen him aren't sages or kings. They're a cowherd and a woman fetching water, doing ordinary work. The fierce archer of the opening is also the light on everyone's morning chores. On the hymn's terms, no special training is needed to see him, only looking up. And that small phrase: seen, may he be kind. As if being seen is part of the relationship. We met the blue throat in the sahasranama, with the churning of the ocean. The Rudram doesn't tell that story. It just calls him the blue-throated one, and moves on.
screen: `COPPER, RED, BROWN — AUSPICIOUS.` · `THE BLUE-THROATED ONE, GLOWING.` · `THE COWHERDS HAVE SEEN HIM.` · `SEEN, MAY HE BE KIND.` · then, large: `ONLY LOOKING UP.`

segments.voice: Sit where there's some light, from a window or a lamp, and let your eyes rest near it without staring: notice its color, warm or cool, and where it falls, on your hands, on the floor. Remember the cowherd and the woman with the water pot, who saw what the hymn saw without stopping their work. If you pray, you can greet the light as the hymn does, as Rudra, as Shiva.
The Rudram. Today's passage: the copper-red one crossing the sky, seen by the cowherds and the women carrying water.
Your line: the Rudram. The fierce one crosses the sky in plain view. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Rudram is chanted in Sanskrit, in a fixed Vedic intonation passed from teacher to student; some Hindus chant it at dawn, and the sun appears in its opening section as a form of Rudra.

chat.says: In that old hymn to Rudra, who gets to see him? Only priests?
options: No: it names cowherds and women carrying water. All beings have seen him.
Yes: it says only priests trained in the chant can ever see him.
No: it says nobody sees him, since he hides deep in a mountain cave.
chat.meaning: The Rudram points to the copper-red one crossing the sky and says the cowherds, the water-carrying women and all beings have seen him.
